title: The Dog and the Sparrow
paragraphs: A shepherd’s dog had a master who paid him no attention and often left him to go terribly hungry. Finally he could stand it no longer. He ran away, feeling miserable and downhearted. On the road he met a sparrow, who asked him, “Why so gloomy, my friend?” “Because,” said the dog, “I’m starving, and I have nothing to eat.” “If that’s all it is,” said the sparrow, “come with me to the next town, and I’ll get you plenty of food in no time.” So the two of them set off together for the town. When they came to a butcher’s shop, the sparrow said to the dog, “Wait here a moment while I peck a piece of meat down for you.” She settled on the shelf, glanced carefully around to be sure nobody was watching, and then pecked and scratched at a steak lying near the edge, until at last it dropped to the ground. The dog snatched it up, hurried off into a corner with it, and gobbled it down. “Well,” said the sparrow, “you can have more if you like. Come along to the next shop, and I’ll peck down another steak for you.” When the dog had finished that one too, the sparrow said, “Well, my good friend, have you had enough now?” “I’ve had plenty of meat,” he answered, “but I’d like a bit of bread to follow it.” “Then come with me,” said the sparrow, “and you’ll have that too.” She led him to a baker’s shop and pecked at two rolls lying in the window until they tumbled out. The dog still wanted more, so she took him to another shop and pecked down some more for him. When he had eaten that, the sparrow asked whether he’d had enough yet. “Yes,” he said, “and now let’s take a walk out of town for a bit.” So they went out together onto the high road. But the weather was warm, and they hadn’t gone far when the dog said, “I’m very tired—I’d like to take a nap.” “All right,” said the sparrow, “go ahead. Meanwhile I’ll sit in that bush.” So the dog stretched out on the road and fell fast asleep. While he slept, a carter came along with a cart drawn by three horses and loaded with two barrels of wine. The sparrow saw that the carter wasn’t going to steer aside, but meant to keep to the rut where the dog lay and drive right over him. She called out, “Stop! Stop, Mr Carter, or you’ll be sorry!” But the carter muttered, “Sorry, indeed! What could you do to me?” He cracked his whip and drove the cart over the poor dog, and the wheels crushed him to death. “There,” cried the sparrow, “you cruel villain, you’ve killed my friend the dog. Now listen to what I say. This deed will cost you everything you own.” “Do your worst, and welcome,” said the brute. “What harm can you do me?” And he drove on. But the sparrow crept in under the cover of the cart and pecked at the bung of one of the barrels until she had worked it loose, and all the wine ran out without the carter noticing. At last he looked back and saw the cart dripping and the barrel completely empty. “What an unlucky wretch I am!” he cried. “Not wretched enough yet!” said the sparrow. She landed on the head of one of the horses and pecked at him until he reared up and kicked. When the carter saw this, he pulled out his hatchet and swung at the sparrow, meaning to kill her. She flew away, and the blow fell on the poor horse’s head with such force that he dropped dead. “What an unlucky wretch I am!” he cried. “Not wretched enough yet!” said the sparrow. The carter went on with the two remaining horses, and she crept under the cover of the cart again and pecked out the bung of the second barrel, so that all the wine ran out. When the carter saw it, he cried out again, “What a miserable wretch I am!” But the sparrow answered, “Not wretched enough yet!” and landed on the head of the second horse and pecked at him too. The carter ran up and struck at her with his hatchet again. Away she flew, and the blow fell on the second horse and killed him on the spot. “What an unlucky wretch I am!” he said. “Not wretched enough yet!” said the sparrow, and she settled on the third horse and began pecking at him as well. The carter was wild with fury. Without looking or thinking what he was doing, he struck at the sparrow once more, and killed his third horse just as he had the other two. “Alas, what a miserable wretch I am!” he cried. “Not wretched enough yet!” answered the sparrow as she flew off. “Now I’ll plague and punish you at your own house.” The carter had no choice but to leave his cart standing where it was and go home, bursting with rage and bitterness. “Oh,” he said to his wife, “what bad luck has struck me! My wine is all spilled, and all three of my horses are dead.” “Oh, husband,” she replied, “and a wicked bird has come into the house, and I’m sure she has brought every bird in the world along with her. They’ve fallen on our corn in the loft and are eating it up at a terrible rate!” The husband ran upstairs and saw thousands of birds sitting on the floor eating his corn, with the sparrow in the middle of them. “What an unlucky wretch I am!” cried the carter, for he saw that almost all the corn was gone. “Not wretched enough yet!” said the sparrow. “Your cruelty will cost you your life yet!” And away she flew.

The carter had now lost everything he owned. He went down to his kitchen, still not sorry for what he had done, and sat angrily and sullenly in the chimney corner. But the sparrow perched outside the window and cried, “Carter! Your cruelty will cost you your life!” He leapt up in a rage, grabbed his hatchet and hurled it at the sparrow. It missed her and only smashed the window. The sparrow hopped inside, landed on the window seat and cried, “Carter! It will cost you your life!” Now he was blind and mad with rage, and he struck the window seat so hard that he split it in two. As the sparrow flew from place to place, the carter and his wife grew so furious that they smashed all their furniture—mirrors, chairs, benches, the table, and finally even the walls—without ever touching the bird. In the end, though, they caught her. “Shall I kill her right now?” said the wife. “No,” he cried, “that would be letting her off too lightly. She’ll die a much crueler death. I’m going to eat her.” But the sparrow began to flutter about and stretch out her neck, and she cried, “Carter! It will cost you your life yet!” At that he could wait no longer. He handed his wife the hatchet and cried, “Wife, strike the bird and kill her right here in my hand.” The wife struck, but she missed her aim and hit her husband on the head, and he fell down dead. And the sparrow flew peacefully home to her nest.
